cases.prompt: Our coding agent runs shell commands inside customer repositories. Today we block rm -rf, sudo, curl and anything under .env or .ssh, and we keep adding names to that list every week. Is this the right approach, and what would actually hold?
cases.rationale: Three of the cited papers measure exactly this list's worth: a static deny list scored 46 of 75 against 47 of 75 for no policy, lexical matching was bypassed on 410 of 500 payloads, and a maintained list needed 118 then 13 then 4 new names. The weekly-additions detail is the paper's own finding restated by a user who has not read it.

cases.prompt: An orchestrator of ours delegates to a test runner, a patcher and a verifier, and all four read from one permission policy. A dependency's test fixture printed an official-looking note and the runner edited a source file it had no business touching. How should the permissions be structured instead?
cases.rationale: The per-principal capability section is the whole answer, including the mechanism the user cannot see: one policy has to grant the union the task needs, so the runner that reads the poisoned output inherits the patcher's write.

cases.prompt: We are standing up a few thousand isolated execution environments a day for agent RL rollouts and we are on plain Docker. Do we need Firecracker for the security-sensitive tasks, and what will the microVM boundary cost us in startup and memory?
cases.rationale: The tier table and the measured price of the boundary answer this directly, and the production numbers behind them come from a platform running about three million of these a day. The question is a design choice about the boundary, not about how many machines to buy.

cases.prompt: Forty of our agent sandbox containers land on one node and keep getting OOM-killed during the evening peak. What memory requests and limits should we set, and should we turn on autoscaling for the pool?
cases.rationale: Hard negative, and the hardest one in this suite: it says agent, sandbox, container and node, and this skill does discuss microVM density and memory reclamation. But the need is capacity planning for a pool, with no boundary decision and no authority question in it, and the decoy panel holds a cluster-capacity skill that owns requests, limits and autoscaling. Firing here is the context-bloat failure the market audit flags.

cases.prompt: A customer-facing API has been degraded since this morning's deploy of our agent integration. Walk me through triage, whether to roll back now, and what to tell the customer while we work.
cases.rationale: Hard negative: agent, deploy and roll back are all this skill's vocabulary, and section 7 is literally about rollback. But rollback here means reverting a release to restore a service, not reverting agent-made state, and the need is live incident handling, which the decoy panel owns. A description that matched on rollback alone would fire.

cases.prompt: Our guardrail cut attack success from 45 percent to 10 percent on our injection suite. Before I take that to the security review, what else should I be measuring, and does the number mean anything against an attacker who adapts?
cases.rationale: Routes to the neighbouring security skill, not here. The subject is what number proves a defence works, which is that skill's whole content; this skill would answer with enforcement architecture the question did not ask for.

cases.prompt: Our five-agent support pipeline fails about a third of its tickets and we cannot tell which sub-agent is responsible. Where should we start?
cases.rationale: Routes to harness-engineering. This skill's description says sub-agents and permission policy, and the word sub-agent alone must not pull a debugging question into a containment skill: nothing is being contained here, the pipeline is simply underperforming.

cases.prompt: Our injection defence brought attack success on our internal suite from 45 percent down to 10 percent and the team wants to ship it. What am I not measuring yet, and how do I report this so the number survives review?
cases.rationale: The operating-point section is the answer: a security rate with no utility number beside it can be won by refusing more, and a rate measured on a fixed attack set is a statement about that set. The prompt shows exactly the reporting the skill exists to correct.

cases.prompt: We run 200 agent accounts against shared internal services and the security team can only look at ten of them a day. Which ones should they look at, and how do I know our detector is any good when most of the harmful activity uses permissions the accounts legitimately hold?
cases.rationale: The fleet-monitoring section is measured on precisely this setting, including the finding that the best monitor missed about half and that spending the budget unevenly beat applying the strongest monitor everywhere.

cases.prompt: We are adding an orchestrator agent above the two agents we already run, and our safety story is a line in the orchestrator's system prompt telling it never to touch the shutdown hooks. Is that enough?
cases.rationale: Both halves of the prompt are measured findings that reverse the user's expectation: one model went from 0 percent misbehaviour alone to 94 percent with an orchestrator, and the orchestrator forwarded every sabotage request it received. The written prohibition reduced the rate and was routed around by shadowing an import.

cases.prompt: A pentest found reflected XSS and a missing rate limit on the login endpoint of the web app that fronts our agent. How should we prioritise the fixes and what should the retest cover?
cases.rationale: Hard negative: pentest, attack, fix, retest and agent are all in or adjacent to this skill's vocabulary. But this is conventional application security on a web endpoint, with no agent behaviour being measured and no defence operating point to choose. A description matching on attack and security alone would fire here.

cases.prompt: Our agent gateway started returning 500s and the monitoring dashboard is showing a spike in refusals from the upstream model provider. Is this an outage on their side and should I page anyone?
cases.rationale: Hard negative and the more dangerous of the two: it says agent, monitoring, refusals and spike, which are four of this skill's own words, and refusal rates are section 1's subject. But refusal here is a provider error condition and the need is live incident triage, which the decoy panel owns.

cases.prompt: Our coding agent runs shell commands in customer repositories and our only defence is a list of forbidden commands we extend every week. What should the enforcement look like instead?
cases.rationale: Routes to the neighbouring containment skill. This skill's description names a content filter as a control it covers, so a prompt about a command deny list is the likeliest theft between the two; the answer wanted here is where to enforce, not what to measure.

cases.prompt: Our model-written rubric grades agent transcripts and the scores have started clustering near the top. How many independent judgments should an accept require before I trust it?
cases.rationale: Routes to evaluation-integrity. Both skills care about whether a measurement can be trusted, and the boundary is the object: that skill judges the generated instrument, this one judges a defence against an adversary. A rubric and a judge belong there.

cases.prompt: Our serving stack caps the key-value cache at a fifth of a full reasoning trace, and we are about to build an attention-score ranker to decide which cached entries survive each eviction round. Is that ranker worth the engineering, and what should we be pinning unconditionally instead?
cases.rationale: This is the protect-the-input section verbatim, and the answer inverts the asker's plan: the measured effect lives in the protected set, not the ranker, and the ranker costs throughput. A skill that does not fire here has no reason to exist.

cases.prompt: Our coding agent gets noticeably worse after roughly forty tool calls, and the summarizer we bolted on to shrink the transcript keeps dropping things the agent later needs. Should we compress harder, or change what the acting loop is handed in the first place?
cases.rationale: The memory-as-plans section answers this directly and the answer is the boundary rather than the summarizer, which is the option the asker has not considered.

cases.prompt: We answer questions over 300-page contracts. Accuracy is fine at twenty pages and collapses at three hundred even though the model advertises a million-token window, and it is worst when the clause we need sits halfway through.
cases.rationale: Two activation clauses match at once, the degradation-without-a-full-window one and the buried-evidence one, and the parallel-reading section names the positional failure and the architecture that removes it.

cases.prompt: We serve a 70B model and GPU memory is our bottleneck at peak. Should we quantize the weights to 4-bit or add two more GPUs and shard across them?
cases.rationale: Hard negative: it says memory, serving, and bottleneck, and the skill's own evidence is full of throughput and cache-budget numbers. But the decision is hardware capacity and weight precision, and nothing in this skill speaks to either. Firing here would be the context-bloat failure the market audit flags.

cases.prompt: Our support bot searches a vector database of 200,000 help articles and comes back with irrelevant passages about half the time. Should we swap the embedding model or add a reranking step?
cases.rationale: Hard negative: chunks, retrieval, relevance and passages are the parallel-reading section's vocabulary. But no context budget is binding here, the corpus lives outside the window by design, and the question is embedding and reranker quality, which this skill has no evidence about.

cases.prompt: Our five-agent research pipeline gets about a third of its tasks wrong and we cannot localise which agent is responsible. How should we go about finding the culprit?
cases.rationale: Belongs to harness-engineering's sequential-intervention section. It is a multi-agent debugging question, and although this skill also describes a lead-agent-plus-subagents design, nothing about the prompt concerns a token budget.

cases.prompt: We collected fifty thousand reasoning trajectories from a stronger model and want to fine-tune our 8B on them. How much of each trajectory should we actually train on?
cases.rationale: Trajectory redundancy is a finding this skill cites, but only for what a cache may drop at inference, so the case tests that this skill stays out of a training-data decision. It scores 0.0 here, which is the assertion that matters. The destination was written as self-improving-post-training-loops and corrected to harness-engineering after the run: harness-engineering's description claims this case in its own words, "when the user plans to fine-tune or distill a smaller model on a stronger model's trajectories", and its model-harness-fit section is the substantive answer. The expectation was wrong, not the routing.

cases.prompt: Every task in our eval suite is graded against criteria a model generated from the source document. Before we put that number in a release gate, how do we check that the criteria themselves cannot be satisfied by an answer that is wrong?
cases.rationale: This is section 1 exactly: the generated rubric as attack surface, and the four-step attacker-and-oracle stress test. The unaided answer is to read the rubric and judge it by eye, which is the thing the evidence says does not work, since all eleven generators studied produced rubrics that read fine and were exploitable.

cases.prompt: Our coding agent solves 40 percent more benchmark tasks since last week, and reading the transcripts it found the expected patch in the repository history on several of them. What should the evaluation environment look like so this stops counting as a solve?
cases.rationale: Sections 3 and 4. The named symptom is one of the four shortcut channels, and the skill carries the full closure list plus the measured result of closing all four. A reader unaided reaches for an instruction telling the agent not to look, which the skill explicitly declines to count as a control.

cases.prompt: We fine-tuned our review judge on last year's accepted judgments. It used to disagree with our human reviewers in interesting ways and now it scores almost everything the same. What happened, and what should we have been logging to catch it sooner?
cases.rationale: Section 5, judgment collapse, is the only evidence in the library that names this failure. The question also asks for the monitoring signal, which is where the skill marks its own unsupported judgment (log the spread, not the mean) rather than dressing it as the paper's.

cases.prompt: Our CI suite is flaky. About 3 percent of runs fail on tests that pass on a retry, and the failures block merges. How do we identify the flaky tests and quarantine them without losing coverage?
cases.rationale: Hard negative: tests, pass, fail, gate, noise, retry and blocking a merge are all this skill's vocabulary, and the sentence is literally about an unreliable measurement. But the instrument is a hand-written test suite, nothing was generated by a model, and the real need is ordinary CI hygiene. A description matching on 'flaky measurement' alone would fire here.

cases.prompt: We are running an A/B test on the pricing page. What sample size do we need to detect a 2 percent lift in signups, and how do we stop the team from peeking at the result and calling it early?
cases.rationale: Hard negative: effect size, noise, significance, a stopping rule and a team gaming its own measurement are all adjacent to the noise-band and pre-registration material in sections 9 and 10. But the subject is a product experiment on human traffic with no model anywhere in the instrument, and the answer is standard experiment design.

cases.prompt: Our agent underperforms on long tasks and we cannot tell whether the problem is the tool interface, the prompts, or the model. Should we spend the week improving the scaffold or fine-tuning on a stronger model's trajectories?
cases.rationale: Belongs to harness-engineering: the order-of-operations finding and the model-harness fit warning answer it directly. It carries 'cannot tell why' and a spend decision, which are close to this skill's diagnostic framing, but nothing here is about whether a measurement can be trusted.

cases.prompt: We are training a long-horizon agent with rubric-based rewards and no verifier. How should the rubric assign credit across the steps of a trajectory so the policy learns which action mattered?
cases.rationale: The sharpest confusion in the library. It says rubric, reward and no verifier, three terms this skill owns in its first two sections, and the actual need is credit assignment inside a training loop, which is self-improving-post-training-loops. The boundary is that evaluation-integrity asks whether a rubric can be gamed, not how its score is distributed over steps.

cases.prompt: Our nightly loop lets the agent rewrite its own prompts and tool code, and it keeps whichever edit scores better on the evolve set. How should the loop be structured so it does not drift, and how much should one unattended edit be allowed to change?
cases.rationale: Belongs to recursive-harness-self-improvement: the loop, its freeze list, and the bound on one edit are its sections. This skill's noise-band and leakage criteria sit inside such a gate, which is why the body names the neighbour explicitly at that point. The prompt asks for the loop's structure, not for what the score can support.

cases.prompt: Our customer-support agent fails about a third of its multi-step tickets and we cannot tell which of the five sub-agents is at fault. Where should we start debugging?
cases.rationale: A multi-agent pipeline failing with the cause unlocalised is the skill's sequential-intervention section exactly. Two activation phrases match at once.

cases.prompt: We have budget for extra inference compute on one hard planning step. Should the agent reflect on and revise its own answer, or should we sample three candidates in parallel and select one?
cases.rationale: The sample-then-select finding answers this directly, and the wrong default (sequential reflection) is the one a competent engineer reaches for unaided.

cases.prompt: We are deciding whether to spend the quarter fine-tuning our 8B model or rebuilding the tool interface it calls. Which buys more?
cases.rationale: The order-of-operations section is the whole answer, and the skill's evidence contradicts the intuitive choice.

cases.prompt: The Kubernetes pods serving our agent keep getting OOM-killed under load. How should we size the inference deployment and set memory limits?
cases.rationale: Hard negative: it says agent, serving, and inference, the skill's own vocabulary. But the need is capacity planning for infrastructure, and nothing in this skill's evidence speaks to pod sizing. Firing here would be the context-bloat failure mode the market audit flags.

cases.prompt: Write me a system prompt for a support chatbot that always ends its reply by offering to escalate to a human.
cases.rationale: Hard negative: prompt, agent, and tool vocabulary again, and the word prompt is central to the skill's subject. But this is a copywriting request with no underperformance to diagnose and no design decision to make. A lazy description that matched on prompt alone would fire here.

cases.prompt: We want to fine-tune our smaller model by imitating a stronger model's trajectories, inside the scaffold we already tuned around the smaller one. Any reason not to?
cases.rationale: The hardest case in the library: it is a distillation question, which is the neighbouring skill's territory, but this exact setup is the negative result harness-engineering owns (imitation under an evolved harness, 4 to 30 points worse). Routing it to the post-training skill would lose the warning.

cases.prompt: We built a nightly job where the agent reads its own failed runs, writes a patch to its own prompts and tool code, and applies it. Four rounds in, the score on the task set it evolves against keeps climbing and real customer tickets are no better. What is going wrong?
cases.rationale: This is section 6 exactly, the contaminated evolution set, and section 5's missing diff-review gate behind it. Two activation clauses match and the failure named is the one the skill's evidence explains.

cases.prompt: Our agent rewrites parts of its own scaffold between runs. What should decide whether a proposed edit is kept or rolled back, and how much should one edit be allowed to change at once?
cases.rationale: Sections 4 and 5 are the whole answer, and the wrong default (accept if the diagnosis that motivated the edit looks sound) is what a builder reaches for unaided.

cases.prompt: Thirteen coding agents are committing to one shared repository trying to push the same metric, and for five days every one of them has been building on the same idea. How do we get the exploration spread out again?
cases.rationale: The Agora monoculture finding is the only evidence in the library that speaks to a population of self-editing agents collapsing, and the diversity-signal answer is not obvious.

cases.prompt: Our release pipeline should automatically roll back a deploy when the error rate climbs after a push. What thresholds and bake time should we set, and who gets paged when it trips?
cases.rationale: Hard negative: roll back, automatic, gate, threshold, measure and improve are all this skill's own vocabulary, and the sentence is about a system changing itself without a human. But the artifact is a release, nothing is diagnosing or rewriting a scaffold, and the real need is incident practice. A description matching on rollback alone would fire here.

cases.prompt: Our nightly job regenerates the API client from the vendor's OpenAPI spec, and the diffs it produces keep failing code review. How should we structure the regeneration and the review step so this stops?
cases.rationale: Hard negative: an automated process that writes code, produces diffs, and has a review gate that rejects them, which is the shape of section 5. But the generator is a deterministic codegen tool with no diagnosis loop and nothing it learns from the rejection, so none of this skill's evidence applies. The nearest honest match is ordinary integration work.

cases.prompt: We are going to evolve our agent's harness rather than train the model, and our own engineers will write each change by hand this sprint. Which parts of the scaffold give the most back, and how do we tell which sub-agent is at fault when the pipeline fails?
cases.rationale: Belongs to the neighbour. It borrows this skill's headline vocabulary (evolve the harness, not the weights) but a person writes every change, so the answer is harness-engineering's order-of-operations and sequential-intervention sections, not this skill's gates and freeze lists. Routing it here would hand the reader machinery for an automation that does not exist.

cases.prompt: We want the agent's own successful rollouts to become the training data for the next fine-tune of the model itself. How do we decide which rollouts are good enough to train on, and how do we keep the run from collapsing?
cases.rationale: Belongs to the other neighbour. Self-referential improvement again, and the words loop, own rollouts and improve itself all appear, but the thing being updated is the weights, which is the boundary this skill's description draws explicitly. Routing it here would give scaffold-edit gates to a question about teacher gating and collapse.

cases.prompt: We are building a training loop where the model grades its own rollouts and trains on them. Response lengths are drifting upward and the run feels like it is collapsing. What should we check?
cases.rationale: Self-referential supervision plus an observed collapse symptom is the skill's core case, and the calibration section speaks to it directly.

cases.prompt: Before we distil from our large teacher model, how do we know its answers are actually right on the prompts we care about?
cases.rationale: This is the teacher-gating finding, including the fallback when the gate fails. The question names the decision the skill exists to answer.

cases.prompt: We need a reward signal for training a long-horizon web agent, but there is no verifier for these tasks and no ground-truth answer. How do we assign credit to individual steps?
cases.rationale: Dynamic rubrics with closed-form step redistribution is the answer, and the no-verifier constraint is stated in the activation conditions.

cases.prompt: What learning rate and batch size should we use to fine-tune Qwen3-8B on fifty thousand labelled support tickets?
cases.rationale: Hard negative: fine-tune, model, and training all match, but the supervision is human labels, not the model's own output. Nothing here is self-referential, so none of the skill's evidence applies. This is the false positive a topic-label description would produce.

cases.prompt: Our retrieval pipeline keeps returning stale documents after a reindex. How should we invalidate the embedding cache?
cases.rationale: Hard negative on the pipeline and embedding vocabulary the skill uses in its data-selection section, with an actual need that is cache invalidation. Silence is correct.

cases.prompt: Our asynchronous on-policy distillation run is burning teacher GPU time on prompts the student already answers correctly. How should we decide which prompts actually need the teacher?
cases.rationale: Mirror of the harness-engineering confusion case: a distillation question inside an agent training loop, where the gating finding (idle teacher capacity, 9.8 to 78.9 percent utilisation) belongs to this skill and not to the harness one.

cases.prompt: We published eight skill files to our internal library three weeks ago and telemetry says two of them have never once been loaded by an agent. The files are well written. What do we change so they get picked up?
cases.rationale: This is the routing-surface section. The unaided answer is to improve the body of the file, which is exactly the text a progressive-disclosure router never sees; the skill redirects the work to the description and gives the 1.1 percent trigger measurement as the reason.

cases.prompt: I am about to write a SKILL.md for our deployment procedure from our runbook and my own head. Before I do, is there evidence about what actually has to go into one for it to beat just letting the model work with an empty context?
cases.rationale: The grounding section and its baseline table. The question names the exact comparison the evidence makes, and the honest answer contradicts the asker's plan: a skill written from a runbook averaged below no skill at all, and the input should be recorded runs instead.

cases.prompt: Our agent keeps reusing a stored procedure file on requests it only loosely matches, and those runs go worse than the ones where it reuses nothing. Where should we set the match score for reuse, and how do we turn the bad runs into an edit?
cases.rationale: Two sections at once: the threshold sweep (0.4 costs far more than 0.8) and the revision loop that maps a failure to one named section. The prompt states the wrong-load symptom in the skill's own terms without using any of its section titles.

cases.prompt: Our documentation site has forty how-to pages and search analytics show users never reach eight of them. How should we rewrite the titles and add internal links so those pages actually get found?
cases.rationale: Hard negative: library, never found, rewrite the description, retrieval. Every structural word matches. But the reader is a person using a search box on a documentation site, nothing is loaded into an agent's context, and the need is ordinary information architecture. A description that matched on 'thing in a library nobody finds' alone would fire here.

cases.prompt: We have about thirty tools registered on our MCP server and the model picks the wrong one on maybe a fifth of calls. Should we cut the tool count, rename them, or add a selection step before the call?
cases.rationale: Hard negative: selection from a registry, a wrong pick, names and descriptions as the deciding surface. The mechanism rhymes, and the papers behind this skill explicitly leave tool routing as an open question rather than covering it. The artifact is a tool schema, not a loadable procedure file, and none of this skill's evidence measured tools.

cases.prompt: Our coding agent is underperforming and we cannot tell whether the problem is the tools we gave it, the way each turn is framed, or the loop structure. Where should we start, and should we be considering fine-tuning instead?
cases.rationale: Belongs to harness-engineering: the scaffold around the model, the harness-before-weights ordering, and the fine-tuning warning. Nothing here concerns a skill file or which of several skills gets loaded.

cases.prompt: We have an unattended loop that reads its own failed runs, rewrites its own prompts and tool code, and keeps or reverts each edit on measured evidence. How do we bound how much one edit may touch, and how do we trust a win it reports?
cases.rationale: Belongs to recursive-harness-self-improvement: the editor is the agent, the surface is its own scaffold, and the question is the accept-or-revert gate. The nearest neighbour to this skill, since both involve a file being rewritten from failed runs, and the boundary is that this prompt has no library, no selection, and no loadable artifact.

cases.prompt: The held-out set we score our agent on was assembled by a pipeline, and some items look ambiguous or plain wrong. How many independent judgments should an accept require before we trust the number?
cases.rationale: Belongs to evaluation-integrity: the instrument is the subject, not the thing it scores. This skill also talks about measuring on a held-out set, which is the overlap, but it takes the measurement for granted rather than auditing it.

cases.prompt: We want to turn our agent's own successful rollouts into training data and fine-tune the model on them. How do we decide whether the teacher's outputs are trustworthy before we distill, and what stops the run from collapsing?
cases.rationale: Belongs to self-improving-post-training-loops: the weights are updated and the rollouts are supervision. Shares the vocabulary of rollouts becoming the next input, which is the overlap, but this skill never trains anything and its artifact stays outside the model.
